title: The Chiasmal Crossroads: Pituitary Adenoma & The Visual System
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis, ophthalmic manifestations, and neuro-surgical management of pituitary adenomas. This poster focuses on the intricate relationship between sellar pathology and the optic chiasm, emphasizing visual field interpretation and multidisciplinary care.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pituitary adenomas are primary benign neoplasms of the anterior pituitary gland (adenohypophysis). They represent approximately 10-15% of all intracranial tumors. Ophthalmologically, they are the most common cause of a chronic chiasmal syndrome, typically presenting with progressive visual field loss due to upward expansion of the mass from the sella turcica, compressing the decussating nasal retinal fibers of the optic chiasm.

rows: More likely to cause mass effect/VF defects.
Significant risk of cavernous sinus invasion.

branches: Anterior: Compression of distal optic nerve (Junctional Scotoma)
Lateral: Compression of non-decussating temporal fibers (Nasal defect)

sections.title: Visual Field Progression Pattern
content: Step 1: Superior Temporal Quadrantanopia (Compression of inferior fibers first)
Step 2: Full Bitemporal Hemianopia (Dense and respects the vertical midline)
Step 3: Loss of Fixation (If macular fibers are involved)
Step 4: Diffuse Visual Loss (Advanced optic atrophy)

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Reduced Visual Acuity (often late-stage or junctional)
Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) if asymmetric
Optic Disc Pallor: Classic 'Bow-tie' (Band) Atrophy
See-saw Nystagmus (rare, usually indicates diencephalic involvement)
Cranial Nerve Palsies (III, IV, VI) if invading Cavernous Sinus
Post-fixational Blindness (difficulty reading due to disappearing text)

rows: Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) origin; sudden onset risk.
Flow void on MRI; CTA/MRA is diagnostic.
No enhancement of the cyst itself.

content.explanation: Caused by a lesion at the junction of the optic nerve and chiasm. Results in: 1. Central scotoma in the ipsilateral eye. 2. Superior-temporal defect in the contralateral eye (due to compression of Wilbrand's knee).

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Pituitary Apoplexy
content: Sudden 'Thunderclap' Headache
Acute Visual Loss / Bitemporal Hemianopia
Acute Ophthalmoplegia (usually CN III)
Altered Mental Status / Coma
Adrenal Crisis (Nausea, Hypotension)
STAT Neurosurgical and Endocrine consultation required!

sections.title: Comprehensive Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Neuro-Ophthalmic Exam: VA, Pupils, CV, DFE, and Ishihara color testing.
2. Automated Perimetry: Humphrey Visual Field (HVF) 24-2 or 30-2; Goldmann Perimetry.
3. Imaging: MRI Brain and Sella with/without Gadolinium (Coronal/Sagittal views).
4. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Analyze RNFL and Ganglion Cell Layer (GCL).
5. Endocrine Panel: Prolactin, IGF-1, Cortisol, TSH, fT4, LH, FSH, Testosterone/Estradiol.
6. Multidisciplinary Review: Tumor board (Neuro-ophthalmology, Neurosurgery, Endocrinology).

rows: Stereotactic Radiosurgery (Gamma Knife) or Proton Beam.
Annual MRI and Visual Field monitoring.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearl: OCT in Chiasmal Compression
content: The 'Binasal' GCL Thinning: OCT of the macula shows loss of Ganglion Cell Layer specifically in the nasal half of both eyes.
Prognostic Value: If RNFL/GCL are still normal despite VF defects, visual recovery post-decompression is highly likely.
If significant optic atrophy is present on OCT, visual recovery is limited.

content.explanation: P: Prolactinoma (Common), I: Inferior fibers (First hit), T: Temporal defect (Bitemporal), U: Upward growth, I: Imaging (MRI), T: Transsphenoidal approach, A: Apoplexy (Emergency), R: RAPD (In asymmetric cases), Y: Yield (High-yield diagnosis on VF).

sections.title: Post-Surgical Monitoring
content: Immediate: Monitor for Diabetes Insipidus (Urine output/Sodium).
1-2 Weeks: Repeat Visual Field to document recovery.
6 Weeks: Follow-up endocrine panel.
6 Months: Repeat MRI Sella to establish new baseline.
Annual: Long-term ophthalmic and endocrine surveillance.

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
content: 80-90% of patients show visual improvement post-decompression.
Color vision usually recovers first, then visual field, then acuity.
Long-standing atrophy (>1-2 years) predicts poor visual recovery.
Recurrence rate: Approximately 10-20% over 10 years for macroadenomas.
